papers.title: Does the Workspace Do the Work? A Causal Protocol for Verifying Global-Workspace Computation in a Language Model
papers.abstract: Global Workspace Theory (GWT), a leading theory of consciousness, holds that information becomes conscious when it is broadcast to specialized processes that use it. Building a workspace into a network does not reveal what the trained network computes with it: a module that reports an answer may have combined a broadcast message with its own knowledge, or merely forwarded an answer computed elsewhere, and task accuracy and ablation cannot tell these apart. We introduce a causal protocol that identifies who computes when modules communicate. Its central test transplants a message from another input, chosen so that ignoring, relaying and recombining it predict three different answers. On networks built to relay or to recombine, the test assigns the right computation in every case. Among trained workspace models it finds all three outcomes: one leaves its broadcast nearly unused, and of two models that differ only in their training data, one relays and the other recombines. In AFGW, a language model whose modules communicate only through a learned workspace, a transplanted message yields the answer that recombination predicts in 97% of cases, and its content acts by redirecting what the receiver retrieves from its own memory. The tests carry over to other communication designs and to a known interface of a pretrained Transformer, turning GWT's central claim into a testable property of trained models.

papers.title: A Control-Theoretic Approximation to Predictive Coding Dynamics
papers.abstract: Backpropagation remains the dominant method for training deep neural networks, but its reliance on non-local computations has motivated the search for biologically plausible alternatives. Two prominent frameworks, predictive coding (PC) and deep feedback control (DFC), offer distinct approaches to local learning, yet their relationship remains unclear. Here, we show that DFC arises as a local approximation to predictive coding dynamics near fixed points, with exact equivalence in shallow linear networks and systematic deviations arising with depth, nonlinearity, and distance from equilibrium. We characterize how this approximation, which we call Approx PC, deviates from PC in its activity dynamics, and show that these deviations can be mitigated by relinearizing the feedback controller and approaching the output target through a sequence of intermediate nudges. In networks trained on MNIST and FashionMNIST, Approx PC reaches task performance comparable to PC trained with the same nudges, and weights learned with it transfer directly to PC inference. Our results unify energy-based and control-theoretic perspectives on learning and open the door to applying tools from control theory to the training of predictive coding networks.

papers.title: When Does Depth Matter For In-Context Learning? Adaptive Inference in Deep Transformers
papers.abstract: Transformers perform computations through many successive attention and feedforward blocks, allowing them to learn complex correlations between a large collection of coupled variables. When does stacking successive attention-feedforward computations over many layers provide a computational advantage over a single transformer block? We address this question by examining in-context learning in generalized linear attention transformers. We first introduce a general theory of distributed inference in such transformers, subject to constraints on communication and depth. We show that such systems can exploit internal representations (`function vectors') to infer a latent context variable at increasingly finer scales over its layers. For an in-context linear regression task, the theory predicts that while one-layer transformers without feedforward blocks are optimal for Gaussian priors over the context variable, multi-layer transformers are superior for non-Gaussian, tree-like priors. Trained linear attention transformers reproduce quantitative predictions from the theory. Using causal key-patching experiments, we verify that function vectors in intermediate layers mediate adaptive routing of information. Our results suggest that depth and feedforward blocks enable transformers to implement adaptive inference, and this is advantageous when the distribution over latent variables has hierarchical structure.

papers.title: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control
papers.abstract: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. Periodic inputs induce nonlinear saturation and context-dependent network routing. Although synaptic weights alone show limited discriminative power, they significantly modulate robustness within a given stimulation context, with reciprocal Ia interneuron connections emerging as key stabilizers. The proposed composite metric achieves robust antiphase detection, outperforming traditional phase-only measures while preserving biophysical interpretability. These findings establish a statistically validated, hierarchical modeling approach in which external drive defines the operating regime and targeted synaptic configurations fine-tune dynamic stability, providing actionable guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers and adaptive neuroprosthetic interfaces.

papers.title: When Should Deployed BCI Decoders Adapt? A Resource-Priced Ladder for Frozen EEG Trunks
papers.abstract: When should a deployed MI decoder spend adaptation resources-not only how to adapt under shift? We study a thin control layer outside a frozen encoder: a resource ladder (factory -> Bayesian head -> affine map, with full fine-tune as an escape hatch) governed by regime-aware gating under a utility that prices accuracy, fit time, and label cost. The head is Bayesian in the conjugate sense: a Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior over the class conditional Gaussians in embedding space, updated in closed form (no gradients) as labelled trials arrive. Full estimators, constants, and the reanalysis code are in the companion paper and the ancillary bundle of this submission. Thesis: adaptation should be gated and capped, not always-on and not blindly fine-tuned. Evidence: (i) utility-max gating over-adapts on clean data that already carries session drift; a clean-referenced gate restores low false-entry rates (e.g. dropping the adaptation rate from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the cascade staying on the factory decoder for ~87% of clean cells). (ii) Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matches or exceeds the frozen trunk's accuracy across five encoder architectures (n=155 subject x trunk cells, pooled across shared subjects), at ~23x lower fit time than full warm-start fine-tuning. Always-on baselines favor capping the default below full fine-tune. (iii) In two no-perturbation BNCI session checks the factory model transferred without intervention (no reliable head gain), so the control layer's value under natural drift is cost-efficiency and clean-safety rather than demonstrated accuracy gains. (iv) Adaptation severity does not follow a universal ordinal ladder across datasets, highlighting the need for dynamic gating over fixed adaptation policies.

papers.title: Revealing Pathway Interactions in Network Computations with Complete Path Contribution
papers.abstract: Networks pass signals through many layers of interconnected units, so explaining what they compute means tracing how information travels from input to output and how pathways interact. Most existing approaches analyze only pairwise interactions between components such as units, layers or attention heads. Even when these measurements are combined post hoc into a circuit, they do not capture higher-order interactions along full causal chains (paths) from input to output, and so cannot address how exponentially many paths interact to construct network computation. This leaves a large set of mechanistic questions unanswerable, for example whether inhibitory pathways veto excitatory ones, and how the two combine to yield network decisions. To address this gap, we introduce Complete Path Contribution, a method to decompose the network output into mathematically complete contributions of individual paths to study path-level interactions directly and at scale. Partial summation then induces definitions of contributions for any circuit at any granularity level, with completeness guaranteed at every level. We further present an efficient algorithm that identifies the $k$ strongest paths without examining all of them, with runtime empirically linear in $k$ rather than exponential in depth. By applying Path Contribution to benchmark image classification networks, we quantify excitatory-inhibitory interactions and show how they collectively construct network decisions at a level of detail previously unmeasurable. Furthermore, in an interpretable model of the mouse retina, it reveals how dynamic receptive fields emerge from excitatory-inhibitory interaction motifs among pathways between different cell types in response to time-varying natural stimuli. Overall, Path Contribution reveals how a network's causal pathways interact at scale to transform input to output.

papers.title: Sensorimotor behavior from an untrained brain-and-nerve-cord connectome
papers.abstract: Connectomes map the neurons and synapses of an adult fly's brain and nerve cord, but how much of behavior follows from the wiring is unknown. Here we turn one such connectome into a spiking network of 172,433 neurons with a published brain model's untuned parameters, and run it alone and inside a simulated body. Two fixed rules connect them: odors and looming objects set the firing of the sensory neurons, and the firing of the leg motor neurons moves the legs. Outside the body, a pathway of known function conducts when it supplies a few percent or more of its target's input. In the body, the fly navigates around obstacles to nearly every odor source. A rewiring that keeps each neuron's connection counts and signs reaches far fewer, and the fly's leg commands replayed with the senses off reach almost none. Navigation needs the measured wiring and sensory feedback. Dopamine-gated weakening of the mushroom body's output synapses turns approach to an odor into avoidance, and the learning is associative once one class of olfactory synapse is scaled. An untrained connectome supports a behavior and its learned reversal. The pathways it cannot drive show what the wiring diagram leaves out.

papers.title: Temporal Contrastive Alignment of EEG and Naturalistic Video Only Beats Linear Decoding On In-Sample Stimuli
papers.abstract: Neural tracking, the temporal alignment between a continuous stimulus and the elicited brain response, enables decoding of attention from electroencephalography (EEG), yet its application to naturalistic video remains largely unexplored and mainly relies on linear canonical correlation analysis (CCA). We investigate whether a temporal contrastive model, pairing pretrained VideoMAE features with a lightweight EEG encoder trained on a correlation-based InfoNCE objective, can strengthen EEG-video alignment. Benchmarked against CCA under three generalization regimes, the model outperforms CCA across subjects (leave-one-subject-out), matches it within the stimulus manifold (leave-video-segment-out), and falls behind CCA when extrapolating to entirely novel videos (leave-one-video-out). Because this advantage appears only for seen stimuli, we probe its basis: a sham control shows that a high accuracy does not certify genuine alignment, as a synthesized correspondence fit to the seen stimuli can reproduce it without genuine temporal alignment in the training pairs. This does not preclude practical use: on a downstream attention-decoding task with seen stimuli, the model remains better than CCA since the decoding only requires a strong statistical coupling, regardless of whether that coupling is physiologically meaningful. Using a group-averaged EEG reference, we further show that genuine, generalizable coupling is nonetheless learned, only buried in the noise of single-subject EEG. These results indicate that progress hinges on data scale, diversity, and single-subject denoising.

papers.title: System-level nonequivalence between integrated information and expected free energy in noisy permutation networks
papers.abstract: The free-energy principle (FEP) and active inference describe prediction and adaptation using generative models, whereas integrated information theory (IIT) examines intrinsic causal organization. Can knowledge of a network's prediction in its current state determine its intrinsic integration? We address this question using a fixed one-step state-risk expected free energy (EFE) and IIT system integrated information. Noisy binary permutation networks allow causal wiring to vary while local transition reliability remains fixed. From a homogeneous current state, different architectures have identical complete one-step predictive distributions, and thus identical EFE under common preferences and observation models. Nevertheless, multicycle architectures have zero whole-system IIT integration, while single cycles can be integrated. For an n-unit noisy single cycle with reliability {\eta}, we obtain the exact expression $\phi_s^{(n)}(\eta) = \min\{2\eta^n\log_2(2\eta), -n\log_2\eta\}$. We prove that the minimum-information partition cuts exactly two causal edges, establish a unique interior maximum, and show that, in the large-n limit, the optimal reliability approaches unity, the joint specified-state probability approaches one half, and the maximum system integrated information approaches one ibit. Independent computation corroborates these results. Local surprisal-coordinate identities can be expressed through optimized variational free energy under exact inference, but this algebraic identity does not establish that a neural system performs variational inference. The counterexample establishes a state-conditioned non-identifiability limit for the specified EFE, not an incompatibility between IIT and the FEP. Bridging the two descriptions requires intervention-sensitive information beyond this single predictive distribution.

papers.title: Persistence of Multifractal Dynamics at the Mammalian Neuromuscular Junction Across Extracellular Calcium Conditions
papers.abstract: The neuromuscular junction represents a relevant experimental model for revealing important biophysical mechanisms underlying synaptic transmission. In this work, we revisited the time-series analysis of electrophysiological recordings obtained from mammalian diaphragm neuromuscular junctions. We applied multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis (MFDFA) to assess whether intervals between spontaneous potentials exhibit multifractal behavior at physiological extracellular calcium concentrations and at hypocalcemic and hypercalcemic levels. Surprisingly, we observed a robust, stable multifractal profile across all electrophysiological recordings, regardless of calcium concentration. Therefore, our results provide support for a rich and complex scenario governing neurotransmitter release. Based on these findings, we discuss their biophysical significance and physiological implications.

papers.title: Cultural invariance in music-evoked emotions
papers.abstract: Worldwide, people produce and listen to music to induce, express, and regulate their own and others' emotions. To what extent culture influences the emotions evoked by music is, however, contested. The documented global variation in musical behaviours and emotion concepts suggests substantial cross-cultural differences in how listeners relate to music emotionally, while shared physiology and evolutionary history would predict broad global agreement on the emotional information extracted from music. Some evidence suggests shared processes but experiments on the subject do not represent global diversity in either music or participants. Here, we report a large citizen-science experiment wherein listeners (N = 124,394 in 189 countries; conducted in English) rated their emotional responses to popular Western music and to vocal music produced in mostly small-scale societies drawn from a globally representative corpus (i.e., songs assumed to be unfamiliar in style). We found strong similarity in listeners' emotional responses to music: Average agreement between pairs of countries' listeners was high. Furthermore, across both popular and unfamiliar types of music, emotional responses were shaped far more by individual listeners and the specific songs than by cultural background: Both between-person differences within a country and within-subject differences across songs explained substantially more variance in emotional responses than country-wise differences. Together, these results indicate that a listener's cultural background has only a marginal influence on the emotions they feel in response to music, raising the possibility of universal structure in emotional responses to music.

papers.title: Regime-dependent reconstruction of structural connectivity: an in silico study of spatially constrained modular neuronal networks
papers.abstract: Inferring structural connectivity from neuronal activity is a major challenge in neuroscience, yet the conditions under which inferred interactions faithfully reflect anatomical connections remain unclear. Here, we investigate in silico how spatial constraints in a neuronal network and its dynamical regime jointly shape structural recoverability. We construct modular networks with varying average axonal lengths and simulate spontaneous activity using the Izhikevich model with synaptic depression across a broad range of excitatory strengths and background noise levels. Using Generalized Transfer Entropy, we infer effective connectivity and compare it with the underlying structural ground-truth at the levels of individual connections and global topology. We observe that the richness in the repertoire of activity patterns is highest in an intermediate regime between globally synchronized and noise-dominated activity, reflecting a balance between global excitation and stochasticity. Optimal structural reconstruction generally occurs under these same conditions, although this correspondence depends on network architecture and is weaker in highly modular networks. Together, these results show that structural recoverability depends jointly on network organization and dynamical regime. More broadly, our findings highlight the risks of treating inferred effective connectivity as a direct surrogate for structural connectivity.

papers.title: Hierarchical Latent Structure Learning through Online Inference
papers.abstract: Learning systems must balance generalization across experiences with discrimination of task-relevant details. Effective learning therefore requires representations that support both. Online latent-cause models support incremental inference but assume flat partitions, whereas hierarchical Bayesian models capture multilevel structure but typically require offline inference. We introduce the \textbf{Hierarchical Online Learning of Multiscale Experience Structure (HOLMES) model}, a computational framework for hierarchical latent structure learning through online inference. HOLMES combines a variation on the nested Chinese Restaurant Process prior with sequential Monte Carlo inference to perform tractable trial-by-trial inference over hierarchical latent representations without explicit supervision over the latent structure. In simulations, HOLMES matched the predictive performance of flat models while learning more compact representations that supported one-shot backward transfer to higher-level latent categories. In a forward transfer task, HOLMES additionally achieved above-chance outcome prediction for stimuli with never-before-seen feature combinations, by exploiting abstract shape-level representations learned across diverse training instances. These results provide a tractable computational framework for discovering hierarchical structure in sequential data.

papers.title: Modeling sequential cognitive states via population level cortical dynamics
papers.abstract: In this work, we propose a mathematical framework for cyclic and sequential patterns of brain activity, combining heteroclinic dynamics with discrete neural-field models. Under explicit structural and positivity assumptions on the prescribed activity patterns, we show that the resulting spatially discrete neural-field system supports neither heteroclinic cycles nor nonconstant periodic orbits. Heteroclinic dynamics, on the other hand, arise in Lotka--Volterra-type systems, but these equations do not directly correspond to neuronal processes. To bridge these descriptions, we use a $C^1$ version of the Universal Approximation Theorem to approximate a target vector field by a neural network interpretable as a high-dimensional Amari-type neural-field system. Each periodic solution of the reduced dynamics admits a unique periodic realization at the population level with the same minimal period. For three-dimensional heteroclinic targets, we establish sufficient conditions ensuring that the approximating vector field admits a unique hyperbolic attracting periodic orbit in a trapping channel surrounding the original heteroclinic cycle. As a proof of concept, we apply this construction to a Lotka--Volterra-type target phenomenologically representing sequential network activations associated with focused-attention meditation.

papers.title: Accurate EEG-based linear state-space model of cortical dynamics during a passive motor task with exogenous input
papers.abstract: Revealing the dynamics of the brain in the presence of exogenous inputs is crucial for mechanistic understanding, interventions and regulations. We study state-space mathematical modeling of brain's cortical dynamics using electroencephalography (EEG) data in an experiment with continuous exogenous input. We use subspace identification techniques to model the brain dynamics in a passive motor task experiment. The EEG data were recorded while participants were seated with their wrist strapped to a haptic manipulator. The manipulator imposed a continuous multisine angular perturbation to the wrist as the exogenous input to the brain. Using two subspace identification algorithms, we show that linear time-invariant state-space models accurately represent the measurements, in a latent space, assuming that the EEG data are the models' output. The model is verified and validated using data from seven participants. Moreover, we construct linear maps to relate the latent space dynamics to the neural source space. We verify that the findings of our model align with those identified in previous studies. Accurate linear model in the presence of exogenous input provides a pathway for designing parsimonious and simple controllers. In addition, it enables development of online monitoring, connectivity analysis and control relevant to neurorehabilitation, motor learning, and brain-computer interfacing.
